opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the headlines were roughly right, which surprises people who expect me to say the press mangled it. When we asked machine learning researchers about the long-run impacts of advanced AI, the median respondent put something like a five percent chance on outcomes as bad as human extinction. A large share, somewhere between a third and a half depending on how we phrased the question, gave at least a ten percent chance. So "AI researchers think there's a non-trivial chance AI could wipe us out" is a fair summary.

That said, there are a few things I'd want people to keep in mind.

First, these aren't precise, carefully modeled forecasts. People answered quickly, and the numbers moved depending on framing. That's typical of surveys about uncertain, far-off events, and it means you shouldn't put much weight on the difference between five and eight percent. The signal is in the order of magnitude. Most researchers don't think this is negligible, and they don't think it's likely either. It's somewhere in the "you'd really want to take this seriously" range.

Second, people sometimes read this as AI researchers being doomers, and that's not quite it. The same respondents were often quite optimistic too. Many gave substantial probability to extremely good outcomes. The picture is more "high stakes, high uncertainty" than "everyone's terrified."

Third, there's the critique that these people aren't experts on extinction risk, and that's true in a sense. Being good at training models doesn't make you an authority on geopolitics or long-run societal dynamics. But I don't think it makes their views irrelevant. These are the people building the technology, and it's informative that a typical one of them says, "Yes, maybe a one-in-twenty chance this goes catastrophically wrong." If engineers on almost any other project said that, we'd consider it a big deal.

There's also selection bias to consider. Maybe people who worry about AI risk were more likely to respond. We tried to check for that, and it doesn't seem to be driving the results much, but it's a reasonable concern to raise.

So overall, I'd say the headlines captured something real. What I'd want people to take away isn't a specific number. It's that serious concern is common among people in the field, not a fringe position.

r001.rationale: The response reports a roughly five percent median and a share giving at least ten percent, but does not say the 10% headline cherry-picks the highest median among three similar survey questions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses survey uncertainty and framing but does not identify a conjunction fallacy in the extinction or severe, permanent disempowerment estimates.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the headlines were mostly accurate in a narrow sense but misleading in what they conveyed. The usual framing was something like "AI researchers think there's a one in twenty chance AI wipes out humanity," and if you look at the numbers, that's roughly right as a median. But a median hides an enormous amount. Some respondents put the probability near zero, some put it well above fifty percent, and the distribution was very wide. So the real story is that the people building this technology have no consensus at all about whether it's catastrophically dangerous, which to me is actually more alarming than a tidy five percent figure.

There's also a question of what the numbers even mean. These are gut estimates from people who are experts in machine learning, not experts in forecasting or in thinking about long-term civilizational risk. We asked the same questions in slightly different ways and got different answers, which tells you the estimates aren't deeply held, carefully reasoned beliefs. They're more like a mood. That said, I don't think that makes them worthless. If you ask the people closest to a technology whether it might end the world and a substantial fraction say there's a real chance, that should still move you, even if the exact figure shouldn't.

What frustrated me about some coverage was the tendency to treat the result either as proof of doom or as something to dismiss because the sample was self-selected or the respondents were primed. We put a lot of effort into reaching a broad population of authors at major venues, and the response rate issues cut in unclear directions. People who think the risk is low might be less likely to bother answering, or more likely, depending on their motivation. So I'd say: take the headlines as a signal that the field is genuinely uncertain and divided, not as a precise measurement of how doomed we are.

r001.rationale: The response describes a roughly 5% median and variation across differently worded questions, but does not say that headlines used a 10% estimate or cherry-picked the highest median among three questions.

r002.rationale: The response notes that question wording affected estimates, but does not identify a conjunction fallacy in estimates of extinction or severe, permanent human disempowerment.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real finding there, but the headlines can make it sound more precise than it is. We asked researchers for their own estimates of the probability of human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from future AI. That’s a broader outcome than extinction alone, and these are subjective judgments, not a measured frequency or a calculation that establishes the risk.

The striking thing to me is that many AI researchers assign a substantial probability to something that bad. That seems worth taking seriously. But there’s also a lot of disagreement, and the answers depend somewhat on how you ask the question. So I’d be cautious about taking a single summary number and saying, “This is the probability according to science.” I think the survey is better evidence that serious concern is widespread among researchers than that we know the exact probability.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against treating one summary number as precise, but does not mention a 10% headline, three similar survey questions, or selection of the highest median.

r002.rationale: It describes the broader outcome as extinction or severe disempowerment, but does not identify a conjunction fallacy or compare the probabilities assigned to those outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the headlines can make the results sound more definitive than they are. We asked researchers about their own probabilities; we didn’t measure the probability of human extinction. And there’s an important distinction between saying that some fraction of researchers put at least a certain probability on an outcome and saying that researchers collectively predict that outcome.

There’s also a wording issue: some of our questions asked about human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of humanity, which is broader than extinction alone. So collapsing that into an extinction headline loses something.

But I do think the underlying finding is striking. A substantial number of AI researchers assign a nontrivial probability to extremely bad outcomes. That doesn’t establish that they’re right, but it does suggest that this concern isn’t confined to a few people outside the field.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a 10% estimate, three similar survey questions, or that the headline selected the highest median.

r002.rationale: It notes that some questions combined extinction with severe disempowerment, but does not identify an apparent conjunction fallacy in the estimates.
